newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria post says will be ready for 1999 sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Austria post says will be ready for 1999 sell-off.

text.p: Austria's monolithic post and telecoms monopoly said on Thursday it would be ready for privatisation in 1999, but insisted it could survive as one unit and avoid stinging job cuts.
"If the conditions are right I think we can succeed in bringing the whole business to the bourse in 1999," Post und Telecom Austria AG (PTA) chief executive Johannes Ditz told a news briefing.
But the strict timetable will prove a tough challenge for the group, which was heavily loss-making in 1995, the former Austrian economy minister said.
"I realise that we began our restructuring much too late and were badly prepared in terms of competitivity. We will try to catch up as quickly as possible."
PTA must by law be floated on the Vienna bourse by January 1, 1999 -- one year after the liberalisation of the telecoms markets in line with European Union regulations.
At present the PTA consists of the state postal service, Austria's only terrestrial telephone network and the country's largest bus company -- all of which lost money in 1995.
Ditz dismissed widespread speculation that the three divisions would still be in the red by the time of privatisation.
"We can only come onto the stock exchange with all three businesses in the black," he said.
In 1995 the postal division posted a loss of 4.8 billion schillings ($394.7 million), while the bus service made a one billion schilling loss. No 1996 figures have been released.
PTA also owns GSM, the largest of two domestic mobile telephone networks. It expects the number of its mobile phone customers to increase to some 800,000 by 1998 from 630,000 at present.
Ditz said he wanted to bring in foreign expertise for its mobile phone unit Mobilkom Austria and was seeking a commercial partner.
"We need to find minority partners for Mobilkom, then we will be in a position to increase the market value of PTA," he said. "Learning by doing is the way forward."
Ditz said the overall strategy was to make the group competitive by cutting tariffs, offering new services -- aimed particularly at big corporate customers -- and bolstering management know-how.
But he insisted job cuts would not be a key cost-saver. "I estimate that by the year 2000 we will have 50,000 employees," Ditz said. At present some 55,000 are employed.
Most of PTA's staff are civil servants and sheltered from redundancy by Austrian law.
The postal service is due for a major overhaul and will offer an express package delivery service as well as financial services, Ditz said.
New phone tariffs were also in the pipeline, with peak time prices to be hiked, while calls made after business hours would be cheaper, he said. Internet users would also enjoy significant savings.
But Ditz acknowledged that Austrian phone charges, currently among the highest on the continent, would remain in Europe's top price bracket. ($ = 12.16 Austrian Schillings)
